title: The light of the ten
hookLine: the Ardas turns to the Guru Granth Sahib, the embodied light of the ten Gurus
tomorrow: The five, the four, the forty
last: HELP EVERYWHERE — PRESENT IN EVERY PLACE.

lines: WICK TO FLAME, DOWN THE LINE.
cards: At a candlelight vigil, the first candle is lit with a match. After that, nobody uses a match again. Each person tips their wick into the flame of the person next to them, and the light moves down the line.
By the end there are hundreds of candles, but in a sense only ever one flame, passed along.

Sikhs have used an image very like this for more than four hundred years, for how the Guruship moved from Guru Nanak to the next Guru, and the next. And the Ardas, having named all ten, now says where that flame is today.

teach.h: JOT: THE LIGHT IN THE LAMP.
teach.b: After the tenth Guru, the Ardas goes on: dasaan paatshaaheeaan dee jot, sri guru granth sahib ji. The light of the ten masters, the Guru Granth Sahib. Jot is light, a flame, the kind that burns in a lamp.
In paraphrase, the line continues: fixing your mind on its reading and the sight of it, say Waheguru! And here, for the first time in the Ardas, the whole room answers aloud: Waheguru.
The idea of one light passing on is old.

teach.h: SAME LIGHT, ONLY THE BODY CHANGED.
teach.b: In the Guru Granth Sahib, the bards Satta and Balwand sang that when Guru Nanak installed Guru Angad, it was the same light and the same way; only the body changed.
Sikhs understand each Guru as carrying the one jot in a new body, ten times. Then in 1708, tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship not to a person but to the scripture.

teach.h: THE FLAME NOW BURNS IN A BOOK.
teach.b: The flame that went from candle to candle now burns in a book. That's why Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib not as a book about the Guru, but as the Guru. It rests on a raised seat under a canopy.
Someone waves a chaur, a whisk, over it as it's read. At night it's carried to its own room to rest.
People bow when they come into its presence.
From outside, that can look like honoring an object. Sikhs would say it's honoring a presence: the light of all ten, in one place, still speaking.

how: After naming the ten Gurus, the Ardas turns to the Guru Granth Sahib as the light of the ten masters, and the sangat answers Waheguru aloud; Sikhs bow before it and treat it as the living Guru.

o: a gathering where the Granth is read
light, a flame like the one in a lamp
a written verse the Gurus left behind

games.q: the light of the ten — tap the pairs.
p: light, a flame in a lamp
the whisk waved over the Granth

s: Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib as a book about the Guru
they treat it as the Guru: the light of all ten in one place.
at this line, the sangat answers Waheguru aloud for the first time
bolo ji Waheguru, and the room replies.
the image of one light passing from Guru to Guru is in the Guru Granth Sahib
Satta and Balwand sang that only the body changed.

games.q: you're visiting a gurdwara for the first time and see people bowing to the Guru Granth Sahib. a friend asks why. what would Sikhs say?
o: it's a very old and valuable book.
it's the Guru: the light of the ten, still present.
it's a custom with no meaning.
games.why: Sikhs honor a presence, not an object: the one jot that passed through ten Gurus now burns in the scripture.

practice: If you can, open a page of the Granth, in a gurdwara or on a screen; if not, picture it: the Gurmukhi letters in long lines, the cloth around it, the canopy above.
Let your eyes rest on the page the way they'd rest on a candle flame, without trying to read it all. If you pray, say Waheguru, the room's answer, once, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Jot, light, a flame. Dasaan paatshaaheeaan dee jot: one jot, carried by ten Gurus, now burning in the Guru Granth Sahib.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jot, light or flame; the Ardas calls the Guru Granth Sahib the light of the ten masters.

carryVoice: Your line: the ten in one. One flame, passed along, still burning in a book. Day six hundred twenty.
